barriers.description: Funding agency and IRB requirements constrained the number of planned design-and-test iterations, limiting flexibility to extend iterative cycles.
barriers.justification: External regulatory and funding constraints prevented designers from performing additional iteration and integrating further feedback, hindering the workload of integrating feedback & iteration and evaluating designs over extended cycles.
barriers.reference_excerpt: We planned the number of design-and-test iterations early in the project to satisfy the requirements of the funding agency and Institutional Review Board (IRB). As the project progressed, it became apparent that those assumptions were correct and that to adhere to budget and project timeline restrictions, we would be able to complete the 3 planned iterations.

barriers.description: Logistical burdens (meeting recruitment goals, preparing materials, coordinating geographically dispersed members) consumed resources and complicated UCD activities.
barriers.justification: These logistical constraints limited designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, manage user understanding (through timely data collection), and coordinate multidisciplinary team activities necessary for iterative design and evaluation.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Many of our recurring challenges were related to logistics, such as meeting recruitment goals, preparing and managing materials (ie, instructions, presentations, and design documentation), and arranging a specific time for members and advisors to meet despite being geographically dispersed.

barriers.description: Disciplinary diversity produced disagreement, communication difficulties, and differences in assumptions that were not automatically reconciled within the team.
barriers.justification: Cultural and methodological misalignment among team members hindered the workload of coordinating a multidisciplinary team and maintaining a shared understanding necessary for coherent design and iteration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: However, with disciplinary diversity comes disagreement, communication difficulty, and differences in assumptions, and although these are all desirable elements, they require efforts to manage, for example, by frequently asking team members to state their assumptions.

barriers.description: The volume and depth of formative interview data exceeded the team's analytic capacity within the available time, delaying discovery of important findings.
barriers.justification: Excess data that could not be analyzed in time prevented timely management of user understanding and integration of formative insights into design decisions and iteration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The number and depth of P2P interviews yielded more data than could be analyzed in the time allotted. As a result, several important findings from stakeholder interviews were not discovered until further in the design process, negating some of the benefits of early learning.

barriers.description: Stakeholder samples were limited in diversity and representativeness (eg, patients were all white and predominantly male; advisors were more educated and engaged).
barriers.justification: Limited and unrepresentative stakeholder recruitment constrained designers' ability to manage user understanding and to specify requirements that reflect the broader target population.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The patients we interviewed in our formative research were all white, and two-third were male. Patient advisors were more likely to be educated and engaged in their health than peers, consistent with the general trend that patient advisors are rarely ordinary people.

barriers.description: Staff turnover and staffing limitations meant that only one design team member had participated in most formative activities and thus acted as the primary voice of patients.
barriers.justification: Loss of continuity and few team members with firsthand user exposure hindered designers' ability to manage user understanding, facilitate stakeholder involvement, and coordinate across phases of UCD.
barriers.reference_excerpt: One project member personally participated in almost every interview, feedback session, design meeting, and usability test. However, she was the only design team member who had interviewed patients and was therefore expected to be the voice of patient participants on the design team. Over time, turnover greatly reduced the number of team members who had been present from the beginning of the project and had therefore participated in any formative research activities.

barriers.description: Persistent designer assumptions and biases led to design choices that were not aligned with user preferences (for example, incorporating rewards that users found distracting).
barriers.justification: Cognitive and attitudinal biases prevented designers from accurately managing user understanding and from producing solutions that aligned with user needs, undermining evaluation and iteration workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Designer bias is difficult to overcome, even when UCD methods are used to collect contradictory evidence. In the P2P project, for example, we incorporated rewards based on the literature. Nothing in the formative data contradicted the potential value of rewards, so it was not until testing that we learned that most participants thought the rewards were distracting.

barriers.description: Scope creep and excessive feature complexity led the team to design many features in parallel, reducing time and effort available for each feature's design and testing.
barriers.justification: Overly broad scope and complexity constrained designers' ability to specify clear requirements, produce focused design solutions, and perform sufficient evaluation and iteration on individual features.
barriers.reference_excerpt: As a result, we attempted to include in a single app a large variety of features. We also attempted to integrate these many features to produce a coherent product. Often, multiple features were being slowly designed in parallel, rather than perfecting 1 feature before moving on to the next. These conditions sometimes led to confusion about the purpose of the app. More features also meant less time and effort spent designing or testing each.

barriers.description: Tensions between designers, clinicians, and patients over innovation versus clinical reality led to disagreements about what features or information were appropriate or feasible.
barriers.justification: Divergent stakeholder knowledge, preferences, and clinical constraints impeded designers' ability to produce solutions that both innovated and fit clinical workflows, thus hindering specification of requirements and integration of stakeholder feedback.
barriers.reference_excerpt: In our experience, designers, clinician stakeholders, and patient stakeholders were divided on what was possible for and needed from the product being designed. Generally, clinicians were more conservative, preferring to replicate existing practices and avoid less studied or riskier options. For instance, clinicians were more conservative than designers about how much unedited information and control over its interpretation to offer patients.

barriers.description: Laboratory-based usability testing provided limited external validity and was easier to run, while in-the-wild testing was more valid but expensive and time-intensive, limiting field evaluation.
barriers.justification: Resource trade-offs between lab and field testing constrained designers' ability to evaluate designs in realistic contexts and to integrate longer-term use feedback into iterations.
barriers.reference_excerpt: P2P usability testing was conducted in a laboratory setting... this setting was more challenging because it required participants to test prototypes in a time and place dissimilar from the intended context of use. In-the-wild testing is expensive and time-intensive and may not be possible in every project.

barriers.description: Standardized evaluation methods required adaptation for older adults (eg, simplified SUS, accommodating breaks, handling vision and motor impairments), indicating limited fit of standard tools to the population.
barriers.justification: Lack of suitable, validated methods for the target population hindered designers' ability to evaluate designs reliably and to facilitate meaningful user involvement without compromising data quality.
barriers.reference_excerpt: We adapted the standard methods in several ways, including accommodating older adult participants. For example, we administered a simplified version of the System Usability Scale (SUS) self-report measure, which we developed specifically for older adults. We also discovered challenges that we had not anticipated, for example, a participant having difficulty completing computer-based surveys because of vision and motor impairment.

barriers.description: Using multiple concurrent evaluation methods increased session burden and data volume, sometimes causing sessions to be cut short and slowing analysis and iteration.
barriers.justification: High measurement and data-processing workload reduced the team's capacity to rapidly analyze findings and prepare subsequent prototypes, hindering the integrate feedback & iteration and evaluate designs workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: At times, the multiplicity of methods in a single session resulted in testing sessions being cut short. Moreover, the amount of data collected during testing affected the speed at which the team could analyze usability test findings and prepare the next design for another round of testing.
